content: The CR kit, known as the DEC Primer Mix (Mira Vista Diagnostics, Indianapolis, Indiana), is available for testing Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) virulence genes. However, this test is labeled for research use only, can only be used on isolates, and is not approved by the FDA for diagnosing human STEC infections. Clinical laboratories considering the addition of DNA-based assays to their testing repertoire must establish performance specifications for the assay as required by the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA). Furthermore, reports from such testing should include a disclaimer to inform clinicians that the test is not FDA-approved. Currently, there are no commercially available proficiency testing programs in the United States for PCR assays targeting Shiga toxin genes. However, internal proficiency testing events and exchanges with other laboratories may be utilized to meet CLIA requirements. Some testing procedures overlap between clinical and public health laboratories. For example, public health laboratories may perform more primary STEC testing in cases involving high-risk groups, such as restaurant workers or childcare facility employees. Simultaneous culture for O157 STEC and Shiga toxin testing is recommended. Clinical laboratories should submit all STEC isolates and Shiga toxin-positive broths to public health laboratories for further testing. Before issuing a final report, public health laboratories should confirm that the isolated strain possesses Shiga toxin genes, produces Shiga toxin, or carries the H7 antigen. Public health laboratories may also determine the O antigen or send the isolate to the CDC for O and H antigen determination. Public health laboratories that detect Shiga toxin using immunoassays are encouraged to use a kit from a different manufacturer than the one used by the clinical laboratory whose results they are confirming. They should also request the name of the kit used for each test. DNA-based detection of Shiga toxin genes is not FDA-approved for diagnosing human STEC infections in clinical laboratories. However, public health laboratories may use this technique for confirmatory testing after internal validation. One commercially available immunoassay, the ImmunoCard STAT. E. coli O157:H7 (Meridian Bioscience, Cincinnati, Ohio), can test for O157 and H7 antigens in human stool samples and stool cultures. This rapid assay can be performed directly on stool specimens or on an enrichment broth culture incubated overnight (16–24 hours at 37°C). When performed directly on stool specimens, the assay has an overall sensitivity of 81% and specificity of 97% compared to culture for O157 STEC. However, this test is not recommended as a first-line or primary diagnostic test because it does not detect non-O157 STEC serogroups, not all E. coli O157 strains produce Shiga toxin, and no isolates will be available for further testing at public health laboratories. Laboratories using this test should ensure that specimens negative for O157 STEC are tested for Shiga toxin and cultured for STEC. Positive specimens should also be cultured for STEC. In clinical settings, O157 immunoassays are less useful than enzyme immunoassay (EIA) tests that differentiate between Stx1 and Stx2, which are critical for identifying patients at risk of severe disease. The Vero (African green monkey kidney) and HeLa cell lines are highly sensitive to Shiga toxin due to their high concentrations of globotriaosylceramides (Gb3 and Gb4), which serve as receptors for Shiga toxin in eukaryotic cells. Sterile fecal filtrates prepared from fresh stool specimens or broth enrichments of selected colonies are inoculated onto these cells and observed for characteristic cytopathic effects. Confirmation that the cytopathic effect is caused by Shiga toxin is achieved through neutralization using anti-Stx1 and anti-Stx2 antibodies. Although highly sensitive, this method is not routinely used in most clinical microbiology laboratories because it requires expertise in tissue culture techniques, access to cell monolayers, and specific antibodies. Testing typically takes 48–72 hours. Certain specialized diagnostic methods may be employed by public health laboratories for patients with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) or during outbreak investigations. These methods may also be used for specimens from patients who seek treatment five or more days after illness onset, asymptomatic carriers, or improperly stored or transported specimens. Immunomagnetic separation (IMS) beads labeled with antisera for O26, O103, O111, O145, or O157 are commercially available. However, IMS is not FDA-approved for use on human specimens.
